s (siot); t at the end of a syllable
silent before a vowel; ng at the end of a syllable (ieung)
ch, with a puff of air (chieut)
k, with a puff of air (kieuk)
t, with a puff of air (tieut)
p, with a puff of air (pieup)
kk: a tense k, throat tight, no puff of air (ssanggiyeok)
tt: a tense t, throat tight, no puff of air (ssangdigeut)
pp: a tense p, throat tight, no puff of air (ssangbieup)
ss: a tense, sharp s with no breathiness (ssangsiot)
jj: a tense j, throat tight, no puff of air (ssangjieut)
eo, like the "u" in "fun", jaw open, lips not rounded
eu, like "oo" said with the lips spread flat
ae, as in "bed" (today sounds the same as ㅔ)
oe (ㅗ + ㅣ), today said like "we" in "wet"
ui (ㅡ + ㅣ): flat-lipped eu gliding into i
ga: ㄱ + ㅏ. A tall vowel goes to the right of the consonant
na: ㄴ + ㅏ (also a word: I, me)
go: ㄱ + ㅗ. A flat vowel goes under the consonant
a: silent ㅇ + ㅏ. Every block starts with a consonant, so a silent ㅇ holds the place
so: ㅅ + ㅗ (also a word: cow)
gwa: ㄱ + ㅘ. A combined vowel wraps below and to the right
san: ㅅ + ㅏ + ㄴ. A final consonant (batchim) sits at the bottom (also a word: mountain)
mul: ㅁ + ㅜ + ㄹ. ㄹ at the bottom says l (also a word: water)
bap: ㅂ + ㅏ + ㅂ. ㅂ at the bottom says p (also a word: rice, a meal)
gang: ㄱ + ㅏ + ㅇ. ㅇ at the bottom says ng (also a word: river)
guk: ㄱ + ㅜ + ㄱ. ㄱ at the bottom says k (also a word: soup)
ot: silent ㅇ + ㅗ + ㅅ. ㅅ at the bottom says t (also a word: clothes)
kkot: ㄲ + ㅗ + ㅊ. ㅊ at the bottom also says t (also a word: flower)
ga · kka · ka: plain ㄱ (relaxed, a little air) · tense ㄲ (tight, no air) · aspirated ㅋ (a strong puff of air)
da · tta · ta: plain ㄷ (relaxed, a little air) · tense ㄸ (tight, no air) · aspirated ㅌ (a strong puff of air)
ba · ppa · pa: plain ㅂ (relaxed, a little air) · tense ㅃ (tight, no air) · aspirated ㅍ (a strong puff of air)
ja · jja · cha: plain ㅈ (relaxed, a little air) · tense ㅉ (tight, no air) · aspirated ㅊ (a strong puff of air)
sa · ssa: plain ㅅ (soft, breathy) · tense ㅆ (sharp and hissing, no breathiness)

missions.name: Chat with the market shop owner
Order and talk about the food at a Korean restaurant

sentences.meaning: Goodbye. (Said when you leave and they stay.)
Goodbye. (Said to someone who is leaving.)
Just a moment. / Excuse me (let me through).
How many would you like? (Lit. How many shall I give you?)
Could you knock a little off?
How much is it all together?
One bunch of green onions, please.
One bottle of sesame oil, please.
This one's a little extra, on the house.
Can you handle spicy food? (Lit. Do you eat spicy things well?)
I buy it at the market.
Where are you from? (Lit. Where did you come from?)
Hope you sell lots! (A friendly goodbye to a vendor.)

grammarNotes.text: Put 주세요 straight after a thing to ask for it politely: "(thing), please" or "please give me (thing)". It's the polite 해요체 form of 주다 (to give), so it's right with a shop owner or a waiter. Point and say 이거 주세요 when you don't know the word.

-(으)세요 is the polite, respectful verb ending to use with a shop owner or anyone you don't know well. On a request it means "please do", and as a question it asks politely about the other person; you've already met it in 안녕하세요 and 어서 오세요. Verb stems ending in a vowel take -세요; others take -으세요.
grammarNotes.example: 안녕히 가세요. = Goodbye (lit. go in peace).

grammarNotes.text: Everyday polite Korean (해요체) ends the verb or adjective in -아요 or -어요: -아요 when the stem's last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, -어요 otherwise, and 하다 verbs become 해요. The same form is a statement, or a question when your voice rises at the end. Without the 요 it's casual speech, too familiar for a shop owner.
grammarNotes.example: 괜찮아요. = It's okay. / 괜찮아요? = Is it okay?

grammarNotes.text: Put -이에요 or -예요 straight after a noun to say "it is", "I am" or "you are": -이에요 after a consonant, -예요 after a vowel. With a question word, or a rising voice, it becomes a question. 얼마예요? (how much is it?) is built the same way.
grammarNotes.example: 귤이에요. = It's a mandarin. / 뭐예요? = What is it?

grammarNotes.text: -이/-가 marks the subject, the thing that is or does something: -이 after a consonant, -가 after a vowel. In quick speech it's often dropped, but it usually stays on question words such as 뭐 (뭐가, "what").

To count things, say the thing, then the number, then a counter: 사과 두 개 is "apples, two things". Counting uses the native Korean numbers (하나, 둘, 셋...), and 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷 shorten to 한, 두, 세, 네 before a counter. 개 is the all-purpose counter for things.
grammarNotes.example: 사과 세 개 주세요. = Three apples, please.

grammarNotes.text: -(으)ㄹ까요? turns a verb into an offer or a suggestion: "shall I...?" or "shall we...?". Shop owners use it with 드리다 (to give, said humbly) to offer you things: 드릴까요? is "shall I give you...?".
grammarNotes.example: 뭐 드릴까요? = What can I get you?

grammarNotes.text: Korean often answers with a single word or phrase. Add 요 to it (이요 after a consonant) to keep the answer polite. It's the natural way to answer a shop owner's questions.
grammarNotes.example: 몇 개 드릴까요? 두 개요. = How many would you like? Two, please.

grammarNotes.text: -은/-는 marks the topic, "as for...": -은 after a consonant, -는 after a vowel. It often sets one thing against another, as in "and the apples, how much are they?".
grammarNotes.example: 사과는 얼마예요? = How much are the apples?

grammarNotes.text: -에 after an amount means "per" or "for": how much for one, how much per kilo. After a place or thing it means "at", "in" or "to", the place something is or goes.
grammarNotes.example: 한 개에 천 원이에요. = It's 1,000 won each.

grammarNotes.text: Prices use the Sino-Korean numbers plus 원 (won): 일, 이, 삼, 사, 오, 육, 칠, 팔, 구, 십, then 백 (100), 천 (1,000) and 만 (10,000). Korean groups big numbers by 만, so 15,000 is 만 오천 (one 만, five 천), and you say just 천 or 만, never 일천 or 일만.
Join 주세요 to a verb's -아/-어 form to ask someone to do something for you: "please (do it) for me". It's the same 주세요 as "please give", and adding 좀 makes it softer still.
grammarNotes.example: 천천히 말해 주세요. = Please speak slowly.

grammarNotes.text: Put 안 right before a verb or adjective to say "not". It's the everyday way to make a sentence negative.
grammarNotes.example: 안 매워요. = It's not spicy. / 안 비싸요. = It's not expensive.

grammarNotes.text: -을/-를 marks the object, the thing you like, eat or buy: -을 after a consonant, -를 after a vowel. In everyday speech it's often dropped (한국 음식 좋아해요?), but careful speech keeps it.
grammarNotes.example: 한국 음식을 좋아해요. = I like Korean food.

grammarNotes.text: -도 after a word means "too" or "also", and it takes the place of 은/는 or 이/가. 저도요 (me too) is the quickest way to agree with someone.
grammarNotes.example: 저도 좋아해요. = I like it too.

grammarNotes.text: -에서 after a place says where something happens ("at") or where it comes from ("from"). Compare -에, which marks where something is or goes to.
grammarNotes.example: 미국에서 왔어요. = I'm from the US (lit. I came from the US).

grammarNotes.text: For the past, use -았어요 or -었어요 where the present has -아요/-어요 (-았 after ㅏ or ㅗ, as before), and 하다 verbs become 했어요. 오다 (to come) becomes 왔어요, so 어디에서 왔어요? (where did you come from?) is how Koreans ask where you're from.
grammarNotes.example: 밥 먹었어요? = Have you eaten? (a friendly greeting)
